title: Sort and fold with the STL
summary: Replace an index loop with accumulate and choose the right algorithm for a search.

scenario.briefing: A sensor report sums even readings with a hand-written index loop. Replace the loop with a standard algorithm and choose an STL algorithm for the next question.

objectives.description: Use std::accumulate with a predicate-like lambda.
Choose an algorithm for an existence check.
Explain algorithm cost and iterator behavior accurately.

hints: The lambda receives the running total and the current value.
Add the value only when value % 2 == 0.

misconceptions.description: Keeping the index loop instead of using an algorithm.
misconceptions.feedback: The standard algorithm states the fold directly. Pass the begin and end iterators, an initial value, and a lambda.

misconceptions.description: Using std::find when only existence matters.
misconceptions.feedback: std::any_of stops at the first match and states the question directly. std::count scans the whole range to produce a number.

misconceptions.description: Believing std::sort runs in linear time.
misconceptions.feedback: Comparison sorting is O(n log n) on average. Linear algorithms cannot order arbitrary values by comparison alone.

sections.title: Algorithms replace hand-written loops
sections.body: The standard library provides algorithms such as std::accumulate, std::sort, std::any_of, and std::count. They state the intent directly and are easier to review than an index loop. Most accept iterators and a callable, so the same algorithm works across containers.

sections.title: Lambdas describe a local operation
sections.body: A lambda captures the state it needs and can be passed to an algorithm. Prefer an explicit capture list over a broad capture unless the lambda genuinely needs the whole scope. A predicate should be small and free of side effects.

sections.title: Know the cost
sections.body: std::sort is O(n log n) comparisons on average. std::accumulate is linear. std::find is linear because it scans. Choosing an algorithm is also choosing a complexity, so match the operation to the data size and access pattern.

vocabulary.definition: A general handle for moving through a sequence.
An unnamed function object that can capture surrounding values.
A callable that returns true or false for an element.
A fold that combines every element into one result.

steps.title: Choose the existence check
steps.prompt: A report needs to know whether any reading is negative. Which algorithm states that question directly?

quiz.explanation: std::any_of stops at the first matching element. std::find also works but returns an iterator rather than a yes-or-no result; std::count scans the whole range.

hints: The question is yes or no, not a position.
Look for an algorithm whose name means any.
It should stop as soon as one match is found.

steps.title: Algorithms and complexity

statements.label: std::sort is O(n log n) on average for comparison sorting.
std::accumulate starts from the initial value supplied by the caller.
A lambda can capture local state needed by the operation.

steps.explanation: Algorithms carry complexity and intent. The initial value shapes a fold, and a lambda supplies local behavior without a separate function.
hints: Comparison sorting cannot be linear in the general case.
The initial value seeds the fold.
